1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 1: Data Management. This is Chapter 1 of the DMBOK, and although it only accounts for about two percent of the exam, I want you to give it your full attention — because this chapter defines the language, the principles, and the framework that every other chapter depends on. Get this foundation right, and the remaining thirteen modules will feel far more connected. Let's begin.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's what you'll walk away with after this module. You'll be able to recite the formal definition of Data Management — the exact one the exam quotes. You'll know the six goals and the eleven principles of data management. You'll understand why data is considered a unique kind of asset. You'll be able to describe the data lifecycle and explain why it's modeled on the product lifecycle rather than the systems development lifecycle. And critically, you'll be able to navigate the DAMA-DMBOK framework — the Wheel, the Hexagon, and the Context Diagram — and name all eleven Knowledge Areas. That's a lot of foundational value packed into one chapter, so let's get into it.

1.title: The Definition of Data Management
1.text: Let's start with the single most important sentence in this entire chapter. Data Management is the development, execution, and supervision of plans, policies, programs, and practices that deliver, control, protect, and enhance the value of data and information assets throughout their lifecycles. Read that again, and notice the structure: three verbs about activity — develop, execute, supervise; four verbs about purpose — deliver, control, protect, enhance; and then the object — the value of data and information assets, throughout their lifecycles. That final phrase, "throughout their lifecycles," is the part the exam loves to test, so don't drop it. Also note who a Data Management Professional is: anyone working in any facet of data management, from a highly technical database administrator all the way up to a strategic Chief Data Officer. It's a deliberately broad definition. Memorize this slide.

1.title: Business Drivers & The 6 Goals of Data Management
1.text: Why do organizations manage data at all? The primary business driver is simple but powerful: to get value from their data assets — exactly the way good management of financial and physical assets lets a company get value from those. Failure to manage data is like failure to manage capital: it leads to waste and lost opportunity. Flowing from that driver are the six goals of data management. One: understand and support the information needs of the enterprise and its stakeholders. Two: capture, store, protect, and ensure the integrity of data assets. Three: ensure quality. Four: ensure privacy and confidentiality. Five: prevent unauthorized or inappropriate access and use. And six: ensure data can be used effectively to add value. Notice how those six goals balance value creation with protection and control. If the exam asks "which is NOT a goal," you'll want all six locked in.

1.title: What Is Data?
1.text: Let's get philosophical for a moment, because the DMBOK does. What is data? At its core, data represents facts about the world, stored in digital — or even paper — form. But here's the subtle point the exam likes: data is both an interpretation of the objects it represents, and an object that must itself be interpreted. In plain terms, data needs context to mean anything. Think of the number "twelve" — twelve what? Twelve dollars, twelve months, twelve degrees? Without context, it's meaningless. That context — the common vocabulary and the relationships between pieces of data — is what the DMBOK calls data's representational system. And the conventions of that system get documented as Metadata. So remember this chain: data needs context, context is the representational system, and that system is captured as Metadata. It's a theme you'll see again and again.

1.title: Data vs. Information & the DIKW Pyramid
1.text: You've probably seen the DIKW pyramid — it's on your screen now: Data at the bottom, then Information, then Knowledge, and Wisdom at the peak. Data has been called the raw material of information, and information has been called data in context. The pyramid is a useful teaching image, but the DMBOK pointedly criticizes it on three grounds, and these three criticisms are very testable. First, the pyramid assumes data simply exists — but in reality, data has to be created; it doesn't just appear. Second, by showing a neat linear climb from data to wisdom, it ignores that you actually need knowledge to create data in the first place. And third, it implies data and information are separate things, when in fact they're intertwined and dependent on each other. That's why, throughout the DMBOK, the terms "data" and "information" are used interchangeably. If a question asks for a limitation of the DIKW pyramid, those three points are your answer.

1.title: Data Is an Asset — With Unique Properties
1.text: We keep calling data an asset, so let's define the word. An asset is an economic resource that can be owned or controlled and that holds or produces value. Data qualifies — but it behaves very differently from physical or financial assets, and these differences are heavily tested. The most important one: data is not consumed when it's used. If I spend a dollar, it's gone; if I use a piece of data, it's still there — I can use it again, and so can other people, at the same time. Data can even be stolen without being gone, because the thief copies it while you still have it. Data is durable — it doesn't wear out — yet it's not easy to reproduce if it's truly lost. It's easy to copy and transport. And here's a kicker: most uses of data create even more data, so volumes keep growing. If you remember one differentiator for the exam, make it this: data is not consumed when it is used.

1.title: The 11 Data Management Principles (Part 1)
1.text: The DMBOK lays out eleven data management principles, and it groups them, which makes them much easier to remember. We'll take them in two slides. The first group is "data is valuable," and it has two principles: data is an asset with unique properties, and the value of data can and should be expressed in economic terms. The second group is "data management requirements are business requirements," and it has four: managing data means managing the quality of data; it takes Metadata to manage data; it takes planning to manage data; and — very important — data management requirements must drive information technology decisions. The third group is "data management depends on diverse skills," and it starts with the principle that data management is cross-functional. We'll finish the list on the next slide. Notice the recurring message: data management is a business discipline that happens to involve technology, not the other way around.

1.title: The 11 Data Management Principles (Part 2)
1.text: Continuing the diverse-skills group: principle eight, data management requires an enterprise perspective — it can't just be local; and principle nine, data management must account for a range of perspectives, because data is fluid and constantly evolving. Then comes the group "data management is lifecycle management," with two principles: different types of data have different lifecycle characteristics, and managing data includes managing the risks associated with data. And underpinning all of them is the foundational principle: effective data management requires leadership commitment. Here's an exam tip worth repeating: principle six says technology must serve, not drive, an organization's data needs. The exam phrases this several ways, so whenever you see "technology drives the data strategy," your radar should go up — that's usually the wrong answer.

1.title: Data Management Challenges
1.text: Because data has these unusual properties, actually following the principles creates real challenges — and the DMBOK devotes a whole section to them. Let me highlight the ones most likely to surface on the exam. First, data differs from other assets, which makes it genuinely hard to put a monetary value on, hard to inventory, and hard to assign clean ownership for. Second, data valuation: neither the costs nor the benefits of data are standardized, so value ends up being contextual — what's valuable to one organization may be worthless to another — and temporal, meaning what was valuable yesterday may not be today. Third, data quality, which historically got treated as an IT afterthought — the old "garbage in, garbage out" shrug. There are more challenges — planning, Metadata, cross-functional coordination, the enterprise perspective — but if you remember that data's value is both contextual and temporal, you'll have a frequently tested fact in your pocket.

1.title: The Cost of Poor Data Quality
1.text: Let's talk money, because the DMBOK gives us two numbers that show up on the exam. Experts estimate that organizations spend between ten and thirty percent of revenue just handling data quality issues. And IBM estimated the cost of poor quality data in the United States, in 2016, at three-point-one trillion dollars. Those are staggering figures, and they're memorizable, so memorize them. The costs of poor quality come from scrap and rework, hidden work-arounds, inefficiency, organizational conflict, low morale, customer dissatisfaction, lost opportunities, compliance fines, and reputational damage. Flip all of that around and you get the benefits of high quality data: better customer experience, higher productivity, reduced risk, the ability to act on opportunities, increased revenue, and competitive advantage. Two numbers to lock in: ten to thirty percent of revenue, and three-point-one trillion dollars.

1.title: The Data Lifecycle
1.text: Here's a concept the exam tests almost every time, and it's easy points if you know it. Data has a lifecycle, and that lifecycle is based on the product lifecycle. It is not — I repeat, not — the systems development lifecycle, or SDLC. Don't confuse the two. Follow the chevrons on screen: the data lifecycle runs plan, then design and enable, then create or obtain, then store and maintain, then enhance, then use, and finally dispose of. On top of the lifecycle, data also has lineage — the pathway it travels from its point of origin to its point of usage, sometimes called the data chain. So lifecycle is about the stages data passes through; lineage is about the path it travels. If any answer choice tells you the data lifecycle is based on the SDLC, eliminate it immediately.

1.title: Implications of the Lifecycle (and ROT)
1.text: Focusing on the lifecycle leads to several important implications, and the DMBOK spells them out. Creation and usage are the two most critical points in the lifecycle — that's where data gets its cost and its value. Data quality has to be managed throughout the entire lifecycle, not bolted on at the end. The same is true for Metadata quality. And data security must be managed throughout the lifecycle as well — the DMBOK's phrase is "from creation to disposal," which is worth memorizing. Finally, because organizations produce far more data than they ever use, lifecycle management means focusing on your most critical data and minimizing ROT. ROT stands for Redundant, Obsolete, and Trivial data — the clutter you want to eliminate. So: protect data from creation to disposal, and cut the ROT.

1.title: Data and Risk
1.text: Data isn't only valuable — it's also risky. It can be lost, stolen, misunderstood, or misused. The DMBOK introduces a sharp little concept here called the information gap: the difference between what we know and what we need to know to make an effective decision. And it labels those information gaps as enterprise liabilities — that exact phrase is testable. Organizations get the most value from data that is available, relevant, complete, accurate, consistent, timely, usable, meaningful, and understood. The chapter also name-checks two regulations in the risk context: Sarbanes-Oxley, which focuses on the accuracy and validity of financial transaction data, and Solvency II, which focuses on data lineage and quality behind insurance risk models. If you remember just one phrase from this slide, make it "information gaps are enterprise liabilities."

1.title: Data Management & Technology
1.text: Because nearly all data today is stored electronically, data management and technology are deeply intertwined — but the DMBOK is emphatic that managing technology is not the same as managing data. There's a natural tension in most organizations between the urge to build shiny new technology and the need for reliable, well-managed data. The principle that resolves it: data requirements aligned with business strategy should drive technology decisions — never the reverse. This is exactly why the Chief Data Officer role emerged. The CDO exists on the recognition that successful data management must be business-driven, not IT-driven. And the CDO doesn't just run initiatives; they lead cultural change, helping the whole organization think more strategically about its data. Watch for exam answers claiming that technology should drive data decisions — that framing is almost always wrong.

1.title: Data Management Strategy — Components
1.text: Let's talk strategy. A strategy is a set of choices and decisions that chart a high-level course of action toward high-level goals. A data strategy has to come from understanding the data needs that are inherent in the business strategy — what data the organization needs, how it'll get it, manage it, and use it. In most organizations, this strategy is owned by the CDO, enacted through a data governance team, and supported by a Data Governance Council. The components of the strategy include a compelling vision, a business case, guiding principles, the mission and long-term goals, measures of success, short-term SMART objectives on a twelve-to-twenty-four-month horizon, descriptions of roles and decision rights, program components, a prioritized program of work, and a draft roadmap. And remember the acronym SMART: Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Realistic, and Time-bound.

1.title: The 3 Strategy Deliverables
1.text: Strategic planning for data management produces three named deliverables, and the exam expects you to know all three. First, the Data Management Charter — that's the big-picture document: vision, business case, goals, guiding principles, measures of success, recognized risks, and the operating model. Second, the Data Management Scope Statement, which lays out goals and objectives for a planning horizon — usually three years — along with the roles and leaders accountable for achieving them. Remember that three-year horizon; it's a testable detail. And third, the Data Management Implementation Roadmap, which gets specific: programs, projects, task assignments, and delivery milestones. So the progression is Charter, then Scope Statement, then Roadmap — from vision, to scope, to concrete plan.

1.title: Data Management Frameworks — Overview
1.text: The DMBOK offers several frameworks as different lenses for understanding data management, and Chapter 1 presents five of them. Two are high-level alignment models: the Strategic Alignment Model and the Amsterdam Information Model. Then there's the main event — the DAMA-DMBOK Framework itself, expressed through three visuals: the Wheel, the Hexagon, and the Context Diagram. And finally, two reformulations: Aiken's DMBOK Pyramid, which describes a maturity progression, and the DAMA Framework Evolved by Sue Geuens, which maps the dependencies between functions. The exam concentrates most on the DAMA-DMBOK Framework, so that's where we'll spend our time over the next few slides. Let's look at the two alignment models first.

1.title: Strategic Alignment Model & Amsterdam Information Model
1.text: Two alignment models, quickly. The Strategic Alignment Model, from Henderson and Venkatraman in 1999, puts the relationship between data and information right at its center. Information ties to business strategy and the operational use of data; data ties to information technology. Surrounding that center are four domains of strategic choice: business strategy, IT strategy, organizational infrastructure and processes, and IT infrastructure and processes. The Amsterdam Information Model, from Abcouwer, Maes, and Truijens in 1997, is famously known as the nine-cell. As the grid on screen shows, it's a three-by-three grid: three levels — strategy, tactics, operations — crossed with three columns — business, information, and IT. Its key contribution is recognizing that middle tactical layer for structure and planning, plus an information governance and data quality pillar. For the exam, anchor these two facts: the Amsterdam model is the nine-cell, and the Strategic Alignment Model has data and information at its center with four strategic domains around it.

1.title: The DAMA Wheel
1.text: Now the centerpiece, right here on screen: the DAMA Wheel. This is the image that defines the eleven Knowledge Areas of data management, and it's probably the single most exam-relevant diagram in the whole book. Here's the one fact you absolutely must know: Data Governance sits at the center of the Wheel. Why? Because governance provides consistency within and balance between all the other functions. Arranged around that governance hub are the other ten Knowledge Areas — Data Architecture, Data Modeling and Design, Data Storage and Operations, Data Security, Data Integration and Interoperability, Document and Content Management, Reference and Master Data, Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence, Metadata, and Data Quality. If the exam asks what's at the center of the DAMA Wheel, your instant answer is Data Governance — and you should be ready to say why: consistency and balance across the functions.

1.title: The Environmental Factors Hexagon
1.text: The second visual in the framework is the Environmental Factors Hexagon, and there's a classic exam trap hiding here, so pay attention. The Hexagon on screen shows the relationship between people, process, and technology. And at its center, it places Goals and Principles — because goals and principles guide how people perform activities and use their tools. Around the center you'll find activities, tools, techniques, roles and responsibilities, and organization and culture. Now here's the trap: students constantly mix up the centers. The Wheel's center is Data Governance. The Hexagon's center is Goals and Principles. The exam will absolutely try to swap those two on you. So burn it in: Wheel equals Governance, Hexagon equals Goals and Principles.

1.title: The Knowledge Area Context Diagram
1.text: The third visual is the Knowledge Area Context Diagram, and it's the detailed template the DMBOK uses for every Knowledge Area. It's based on a SIPOC diagram — Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Consumers — and, as the layout on screen shows, it puts activities at the center, because activities produce the deliverables that meet stakeholder requirements. Those activities are sorted into four phases — P, D, C, and O. Planning activities set the strategic and tactical course and recur over time. Development activities are organized around the systems development lifecycle. Control activities ensure ongoing quality, integrity, reliability, and security. And Operational activities support use, maintenance, and enhancement. The full diagram has twelve components, including definition, goals, activities, inputs, deliverables, roles, suppliers, consumers, participants, tools, techniques, and metrics. One precise distinction the exam loves: suppliers enable access to inputs, consumers benefit from the deliverables, and participants are the ones who actually perform, manage, or approve the activities. Know those three apart.

1.title: The 11 Knowledge Areas
1.text: Let's put names to all eleven Knowledge Areas, because the rest of this course is essentially a deep dive into each one. Chapter 3 is Data Governance — direction and oversight through a system of decision rights. Chapter 4, Data Architecture — the blueprint aligning data assets with strategy. Chapter 5, Data Modeling and Design. Chapter 6, Data Storage and Operations. Chapter 7, Data Security. Chapter 8, Data Integration and Interoperability. Chapter 9, Document and Content Management — managing unstructured media. Chapter 10, Reference and Master Data. Chapter 11, Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence. Chapter 12, Metadata. And Chapter 13, Data Quality. That's the eleven. One important note: Chapter 2, Data Handling Ethics, and Chapter 14, Big Data and Data Science, are full chapters in the DMBOK and they're on the exam — but they are not Knowledge Areas on the Wheel. The exam sometimes tests that distinction, so keep it straight.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate the testable numbers from this chapter into one cheat sheet you can photograph in your memory. There are eleven Knowledge Areas on the Wheel. Poor data quality costs ten to thirty percent of revenue. IBM pegged the US cost of poor data quality in 2016 at three-point-one trillion dollars. SMART objectives operate on a twelve-to-twenty-four-month timeframe. The Scope Statement uses a three-year planning horizon. The Context Diagram has four activity categories — P, D, C, O — and twelve components total. The Amsterdam Information Model is the nine-cell. The first edition of the DMBOK was published in 2009, and the Leader's Data Manifesto dates to 2017. If a question hinges on a number, odds are it's on this slide — so review it until it's automatic.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Before we wrap, let me arm you against the specific traps this chapter sets. Trap one: the data lifecycle is based on the product lifecycle, not the SDLC — don't let a question talk you out of that. Trap two, the big one: the center of the Wheel is Data Governance, while the center of the Hexagon is Goals and Principles. The exam will swap them; don't fall for it. Trap three: business strategy and data requirements drive technology — not the reverse, no matter how the question is dressed up. Trap four: data is not consumed when it's used, so any answer implying data gets "used up" is wrong. And trap five: keep suppliers, consumers, and participants straight in the context diagram. Know these five, and you'll dodge the most common ways candidates lose points on Chapter 1 material.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's bring it all together. Data Management is the development, execution, and supervision of plans, policies, and practices that deliver, control, protect, and enhance data's value throughout the lifecycle. Data is an asset with unique properties — above all, it's not consumed when used. There are six goals and eleven principles, and leadership commitment underpins them all. The data lifecycle follows the product lifecycle, and good lifecycle management means minimizing ROT. And the DMBOK framework rests on three visuals: the Wheel, with Data Governance at the center; the Hexagon, with Goals and Principles at the center; and the Context Diagram, with Activities at the center, organized by Plan, Develop, Control, and Operate. Nail those, and you've nailed Chapter 1.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time to put it to the test. Here are five practice questions drawn from the Data Management material. My advice: pause on each one and commit to an answer before you reveal the solution. And read carefully for those qualifier words — "primary," "best," "not" — because they decide the question. Ready? Let's go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one asks for a primary goal of a data management program. The answer is B — to enable the organization to get value from its data assets while managing costs and risks. That's the DMBOK's core purpose statement; the other options are narrow or even counterproductive.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: the four activity types within each knowledge area. The answer is C — Planning, Control, Development, and Operational. Remember P, D, C, O. The other choices are tempting pipeline stages, but they aren't the DMBOK's categories.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three asks for a core component of a data management strategy. The answer is A — a statement of vision, goals, guiding principles, and a prioritized roadmap. The other options are inventories and artifacts, not the strategy itself.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four contrasts the CDO and the CIO. The answer is B — the CDO leverages data as a strategic business asset and drives data culture, while the CIO manages IT infrastructure and delivery. Option C reverses them, which is the trap. And

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: question five: what kind of organization is DAMA International? The answer is B — a non-profit professional association advancing data management practices. Not a government, not a regulator, not a vendor consortium. How did you do? If any of those tripped you up, revisit the relevant slide before moving on. When you're ready, I'll see you in Module 2: Data Handling Ethics.
